source.title: Paloma: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Model Fit
source.authors: Ian Magnusson; Akshita Bhagia; Valentin Hofmann; Luca Soldaini; A. Jha; O. Tafjord; Dustin Schwenk; Pete Walsh; Yanai Elazar; Kyle Lo; Dirk Groeneveld; I. Beltagy; Hanna Hajishirzi; Noah A. Smith; Kyle Richardson; Jesse Dodge

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own scaling measurements and refines the broad scaling claim by showing domain-specific non-monotonic loss trends and unequal improvement rates.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own scaling analyses in Appendix D.1 and its downstream-correlation analysis in Appendix A. Scaling trends cited from Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are not treated as results. The paper’s vocabulary-type analysis is described under fits_no_version because it measures type-level likelihood differences rather than the versions’ stated aggregate loss laws.
record.test_reason: Appendix D.1 measures how held-out perplexity changes with tokens seen (six controlled 1B baselines, ~20B to ~150B) and with parameters (Pythia 160M/1B/7B) across ~546 domains. It finds loss falls on most domains, rises on some for C4- and mC4-trained models, and improves at unequal rates. Appendix A relates perplexity to downstream rankings. These are the study's own results that qualify V1 and V7 and bear weakly on V6. No power laws are fitted, and token scaling spans under one order of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find loss falls with scale on most domains but at unequal rates. C4- and mC4-trained models worsen on dozens of domains with more training, and CC-only models show non-monotonic fit. No single perplexity source tracks all downstream tasks, which contrasts with the assumption that lower perplexity always means better downstream results. They do not frame unequal improvement as a problem, and they call for experiments over wider scales and data recipes.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses controlled multi-domain perplexity evaluations and a limited token/parameter scaling analysis rather than reproducing the original scaling-law fitting and compute-allocation procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with pretraining corpus and evaluation domain; improvement rates also vary across domains and model sizes. The downstream correlations vary by perplexity source and task.

fits_no_version.finding: Relative perplexity gaps between the Dolma, Pile and RedPajama baselines are highly stable through training (Section 4.1, Figures 2–3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rankings of pretraining corpora by domain perplexity are stable across training checkpoints for curated mixtures.

fits_no_version.finding: Pythia-1B has lower mean loss than Pythia-7B on 8.5%–32.1% of vocabulary types depending on source. These are mostly low-frequency types, and some types get worse over training for the larger model (Appendix D.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregate loss improvements with scale mask type-level inverse scaling on a substantial share of vocabulary types.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
record.problems: The controlled baseline scaling runs are all 1B models, so they do not test parameter scaling. The Pythia scaling results do not follow all the paper’s training controls, including decontamination. The paper reports no error bars for its pretraining experiments and states that multiple runs were not feasible. The downstream correlations use only six pretraining experiments, and the authors caution against strong conclusions from them.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A Table 3 reports 128 source-by-task correlations; only selected examples are retained to show variation, with the remaining table entries omitted due to the 60-row cap. Appendix D.1 includes plotted per-domain scaling values and curves not separately extracted where the text gives only aggregate descriptions. Appendix D.2’s type-level result is summarized in fits_no_version rather than given an outcome row because it does not directly measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Power-law functional form, several orders of magnitude, and the non-bottleneck condition. Token scaling spans ~20B–150B only, and no fits are made.
Entire version: no fitted law is extrapolated to larger runs.
Entire version: no fixed-compute allocation sweep.
Entire version: architecture shape not varied.
Entire version: only text and code pretraining.
Downstream prediction across model scale; only six same-size models differing in data are compared.
Parameter counting, training schedule, fitting method, and compute-optimal split are not varied.

missing.what: Aggregate PALOMA perplexity over tokens seen (~20B to ~150B) for all six controlled 1B baselines, which decreases over training. This bears on V1 at the aggregate level.
Figure 8 statement that relative differences between Pythia size curves are 'remarkably stable across all sources'.

record.verdict_notes: Token scaling is two-point slopes over less than one order of magnitude, measured on intermediate checkpoints of a 300B-token cosine schedule. The authors themselves warn such checkpoints scale sub-optimally. Pythia results are not decontaminated. The reader's V2 label (r5) was removed because no extrapolation is tested. The V7 labels were changed from limits_scope to supports, because domain- and corpus-dependent slopes are what V7 predicts. r18 had its source and task swapped.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit power laws over several orders of magnitude in parameters, tokens, or compute, nor does it test the non-bottleneck conditions in the version.
The study does not make quantitative out-of-range predictions from fitted small-run power laws and compare them with much larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
Depth, width, or other architecture choices are not varied at fixed parameter count.
The scaling experiments concern text and code language-model evaluations; no other modality or training regime is tested.
The downstream analysis compares rankings across six final checkpoints trained on different data mixtures; it does not establish downstream prediction across a wide range of compute scales.
The paper shows domain- and corpus-dependent trends, including non-monotonicity, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, fitting method, or compute-optimal allocation choices.

rows.subject: Dolma, The Pile, and RedPajama 1B baselines

rows.subject: C4 1B, mC4 1B, Falcon RefinedWeb 1B, Dolma 1B, The Pile 1B, and RedPajama 1B baselines
rows.operation_detail: Compared domain-level improvement rates between checkpoints at approximately 20B and 150B tokens seen.
rows.measure: Difference between most- and least-improved domains
rows.value: Median difference was 1.57×; it was 1.94× when excluding the C4 and mC4-en baselines.
rows.locator: Appendix D.1.1, Figure 6 and accompanying text
rows.note: These are aggregate differences in domain improvement rates, not fitted exponents.
rows.check: Unequal two-point slopes across domains (median 1.57x, or 1.94x excluding C4/mC4) do not contradict V1. They bear on V7 as evaluation-data dependence of the improvement rate. These are not fitted exponents.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M, Pythia 1B, and Pythia 7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared macro-average perplexity across model sizes and checkpoints.
rows.value: The paper reports that increased parameter count consistently lowered perplexity and that macro-average perplexity decreased faster over tokens seen for larger models in all sources.
rows.locator: Appendix D.1.2, Figure 8 and accompanying text
rows.note: The statement aggregates across sources; the figure contains individual curves. Pythia models were not trained with the paper’s decontamination control.
rows.check: Pythia models are not decontaminated against PALOMA. The parameter range covers about 1.6 orders of magnitude and no power law is fitted.

source_check.correct: Greater parameter count consistently lowers source-level macro-average perplexity; larger models also improve faster with tokens. State cannot_determine for V1's power-law form.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix D.1.2, increased-parameter-count paragraph and Figure 8.
source_check.problem: Monotonic improvement across three sizes does not establish a power law over several orders of magnitude.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M, Pythia 1B, and Pythia 7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared per-domain improvement from 160M to 1B and from 1B to 7B, using non-embedding parameter counts.
rows.measure: Difference between most- and least-improved domains
rows.locator: Appendix D.1.2, Figure 9 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors state that increases in model size improved every domain, but at unequal rates.
rows.check: Every domain improves with model size (observed for V1), while rates differ by domain (median 2.02x), which is observed for V7. Pythia is uncontrolled for contamination.

source_check.correct: Every domain improves with model size; the reported median improvement gap is 2.02×. Observed for domain-dependent slopes under V7; cannot_determine for V1's power-law form.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix D.1.2, domain-improvement paragraph and Figure 9.
source_check.problem: The observed state applies to slope variation, but overstates evidence for V1's functional form.
